pages.title: Gangue
pages.text: Rock is not metal. What a lump of ore yields comes with the stony part that was never metal, and that part becomes slag sitting in your bath.$p$pRich ore is the cleanest at roughly 5-8% of the bath, normal 8-13%, poor 10-17%, and the small fragments you sweep off the ground 12-20%.

pages.title: You Cannot See It
pages.text: Nothing on the item tells you how dirty this particular lump is, and two lumps of the same grade differ a little from each other. The only honest reading is the Slag line in the crucible after they are in there.$p$pMelting refined metal instead brings its own history: flawed scrap keeps the slag it was cast with.

pages.title: So What
pages.text: Smelting straight from rock always gives Flawed metal, because the slag is over the 2% line before you have done anything wrong with the ratio.$p$pThere are exactly two places where that dirt can be dealt with. **Before the fire**: crush the lump, wash the scoops, and the rock never reaches the bath. **After the fire**: a furnace with a tap cut below the floating layer lets the slag leave while the metal stays. Nothing in between - a crucible pours from the top, so its dirt is in the pour, and no tool lifts it off.$p$pWhich is why washing is the habit that carries you from copper to steel, and why the furnace is worth building the day your steel demand stops fitting in one crucible.

pages.title: Crush, Wash, Grind
pages.text: The quern breaks a lump into **crushed ore**: seven scoops from a rich one, five from a normal, three from a poor, two from the small fragments, and every scoop is worth five mB of metal.$p$pMelt a scoop as it is and you get those five mB with all of the stone still in it - about **12% of the bath** - and the lump has lost the one thing that made it worth picking, its grade. Nothing on a scoop says which vein it came from.$p$pSo crushing is only ever the first step of three.

pages.title: Washing Is the Paying Step
pages.text: Four scoops of crushed ore and a drink of water in a barrel come out as one piece of **washed ore**, worth the twenty mB they carried between them: the wash spends no metal at all, it only spends the quern stroke and the water. Four rather than five, so a stack of scoops divides without a remainder sitting in the barrel, and five pieces of washed ore fill one mold to the hundredth millibucket.$p$pAnd it takes most of the dirt with it. Crushed ore brings about **12% slag**; washed ore brings **3%**, or **5%** when the mineral is a sulfide - bismuthinite, sphalerite, tetrahedrite. Water moves grit, and sulfur sits inside the crystal rather than between grains, so the wash cannot reach it: that is what a furnace's oxidising flux is for.$p$pSo the ladder is one step per tool. Raw ore pours **Severe**, washed ore pours **Minor**, and only a tap below the floating layer makes either of them clean. What the flaw system can still reach you through metal you already melted: re-smelting an object keeps its dirt, because metal does not become clean by being forged.

pages.title: The Powder Comes Out of the Washed Ore
pages.text: Put washed ore back on the quern and it grinds into **ore powder** - the same powder TFC has always used for dyes, for kaolin and for the colour of glass - five scoops, exactly what one lump of the raw ore used to give.$p$pWhat it does not do is melt. Metal worth keeping is worth keeping as washed ore, and a powder that also smelted would make the wash a detour instead of a step: grind for paint, and smelt the rest.

pages.title: What Water Really Sorts
pages.text: Weight is what water can tell apart, so the honest version of this chain is the oxide and native ores: hematite, limonite and magnetite, cassiterite, malachite, and native copper, gold and silver are far heavier than the quartz they sit in.$p$pSphalerite, bismuthinite, tetrahedrite and garnierite are barely heavier at all - a real plant roasted and floated those, and here the barrel simply stands in for that work, because this is a game and one barrel is easier to explain than a furnace full of acid.
